The Madagascar tomato frog (Dyscophus antongilii) exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females reaching more than double the snout-vent length of males. Field surveys of adult females have recorded a typical maximum body size of 10.5 centimeters [Li = 10.5 centimeters], although some exceptionally large individuals from the Masoala Peninsula are reported to fall within a range of 85 to 105 millimeters. Males, by contrast, possess a substantially smaller ultimate body length of 6.5 centimeters [Li = 6.5 centimeters], with most mature males measuring between 60 and 65 millimeters. This size disparity is among the most extreme observed within the family Microhylidae and is thought to be linked to the species' reproductive strategy, wherein large female body volume allows for the production of substantial clutches. The size at which individuals attain puberty, defined as the onset of functional gonadal activity, has been estimated at 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters] based on growth trajectories of known-age animals in a captive colony at the University of Antananarivo. This value is derived from the observation that individuals take roughly three years to reach this body length under standard conditions.

Neonatal body mass in Dyscophus antongilii is remarkably low, with newly hatched tadpoles weighing approximately 0.001 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.001 grams] upon emergence from the egg. This minute initial size is consistent with the pattern seen in other microhylid frogs that deposit large numbers of small eggs. The developmental trajectory from hatching through the larval period proceeds rapidly when water temperatures are elevated. Eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C] hatch after only 1.5 days [ab = 1.5 days], a remarkably brief incubation period that reflects the species' adaptation to ephemeral breeding pools in the lowland rainforests of eastern Madagascar. The rapidity of this initial developmental phase is critical, as it allows tadpoles to begin exogenous feeding and exploit transient algal blooms before pond desiccation. In contrast, the timing of metamorphosis is governed by different thermal optima; at a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time elapsed from hatching to metamorphic climax is approximately 45 days , during which the tadpole undergoes extensive morphological reorganization.

Reproductive output in the tomato frog is considerable, a fact that aligns with its large female body size. Females are capable of producing between 1,000 and 1,500 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 1,000 and 1,500 eggs per clutch] under favorable conditions, with some sources extending the upper bound to as many as 15,000 eggs per clutch. When maintained at a stable temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], gravid females may deposit as many as four clutches per year [F_R_i = four clutches per year] during the extended breeding season, which coincides with the austral summer rains. This high frequency of reproductive events, combined with the substantial clutch sizes, places the tomato frog among the most fecund microhylids documented in the literature. The thermal dependence of this reproductive rate is notable, as reproductive activity wanes considerably when ambient temperatures drop below 20 °C, suggesting a metabolic constraint on vitellogenesis and egg deposition. The physiological basis for this pattern likely involves temperature-sensitive enzymatic pathways that govern yolk protein synthesis in the liver.

The ultimate wet weight of approximately 230 grams [Wwi = approximately 230 grams] in adult females is roughly 230,000 times greater than the 0.001 gram [Wwb = 0.001 gram] hatchling mass, underscoring the enormous scope for post-metamorphic growth. Adult males attain a far more modest body mass of 41 grams [Wwi = 41 grams], which correlates closely with their reduced skeletal dimensions. The body mass estimated at the onset of puberty, defined as the point at which gametogenesis commences, has been estimated at 68 grams [Wwp = estimated at 68 grams] for females, a value that aligns with the allometric relationship between length and mass observed in the species. This pubertal mass is achieved after approximately three years of sustained growth, at which point females have typically reached the 7 centimeter [Lp = 7 centimeter] snout-vent length associated with reproductive competence. The transition from juvenile to adult body composition involves a disproportionate accumulation of adipose tissue, which serves as an energetic reserve for the high demands of egg production.

Longevity records for Dyscophus antongilii in captivity, maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of 12 years [am = a maximum lifespan of 12 years], a relatively extended duration for a frog of this moderate body size. Field-based mark-recapture studies in the Analamazaotra Reserve have reported a somewhat shorter lifespan in the wild, likely due to predation pressure and seasonal resource limitation. The growth trajectory following metamorphosis is characterized by a rapid initial phase, with juveniles attaining approximately half of their adult length within the first 18 months, before growth decelerates markedly as individuals approach the pubertal threshold. Comparative data from other Dyscophus species suggest that D. antongilii is the longest-lived member of the genus, possibly owing to its larger body size and the associated reduction in mass-specific metabolic rate. Following reproduction, females enter a period of physiological recovery during which they replenish depleted energy stores before the next breeding season, a pattern that contributes to the species' iteroparous life history strategy.
